about: Decisions the main agent made on its own authority, with what it recommended and where each stands. Andrew, 2026-11-11: "just be proactive and do what you need to do; make a decisions.json file with all your decisions and what you recommended and just do things and get blaze to work". A decision here is reversed by Andrew saying so; one that changes a rule also changes tools/agents/rules.ts.

decisions.decision: When memory is short the daemon gives back in one order, cheapest to make again first, each step measured before the next (`blaze_graph::giveback::Planner`): the allocators' freed pages, the stores' pool pages, caches, a front end's values by bytes, and last one checkout's kept front end. Three behaviours change with it. (1) A system memory-pressure event takes the values of every kept front end and no front end whole; before, it dropped every kept front end. (2) The builds under way are asked for a release (`Writer::short`) only when their MIR and inference are in proportion to what is short (at most four times the need and its margin), not on every task held back. (3) The front end of the checkout built last (the floor) is never dropped: a task whose wait only the floor could meet waits for a task to end or starts alone, and when the limit falls under what the daemon holds with only the floor left the daemon says so by name and keeps it.
decisions.why: lane memgive-1112 (claude-fable-5-2). On 2026-11-12 a task that waited for 0.09 GiB made the daemon drop reth's kept front end (about 55 GiB held of a limit of 67.08 GiB) and the next build, a one-line revert, took 195.4 s where it takes 4 to 16 s; the same night three daemons squeezed each other and each pressure event dropped every kept front end. Rule incremental-first: the edit loop is what blaze is judged by, and a front end is the dearest thing the daemon holds. What is given up: under real pressure the daemon keeps up to one front end it would have freed (the ceiling's guard and admission's cap are still the last line), and a large task may start alone, serially, where dropping the floor would have let it run beside others.
decisions.recommended: Yes. Confirm on reth's daemon with the limit lowered in steps (docs/v2/plan/design/memory.md, "Giving memory back"): no `is let go` line and edits in seconds while the footprint is under the limit.
decisions.state: written on int-1112 (34b4f5600e), not compiled or measured; the coordinator confirmed the three changes on 2026-11-12; the owner has not seen it

decisions.decision: Lanes with their own ix VM build, check and test their own work. Merges to main, measurements that claims rest on, persisted-state and bootstrap changes, and the check before a merge stay with the main agent.
decisions.why: The round trip through the main agent cost 10 to 40 minutes per fix all day; a lane with a VM closes the loop in minutes.
decisions.recommended: Yes, for the speed lanes first.
decisions.state: done: rule fan-out-write-only rewritten

decisions.decision: One new blaze built from today's tree becomes the compiler for all work (a blaze built earlier is a legal stage 0). It is used on the VMs as soon as stage 2 passes; a release follows when main's gate is green.
decisions.why: The old release has its own faults and does not know the lint ratchet or the language extensions; most of the day's detours came from building with it.
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: in progress: stage 2 running on two VMs

decisions.decision: "Compiles" means `blaze check` with tests on the exact tip, by a blaze that knows the tree's rules, before a merge.
decisions.why: Main was merged on a library build by the old release; its daemon tests and its own lint check did not pass.
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: in force

decisions.decision: A crate with no line in a lint baseline is unmeasured (held at warn until a bless records it), not zero. Vendored third-party crates and the std-only script crates are exempt from blaze's own style lints by rule.
decisions.why: A new crate could not pass the check, so could not be blessed, so could never get a line; 3,931 lint errors in script and vendored crates stopped the tree's own check.
decisions.recommended: Yes to both.
decisions.state: partly done: 89 crates listed unmeasured by hand on edit-all-1111; the rule change in blaze-lints and blaze-units is to do

decisions.decision: Memory is a first priority beside edit latency: front-end results become store records read through the pool, and the allocator returns freed memory.
decisions.why: Memory stopped work three times on 2026-11-11 (58 GB for one crate's tests, 81 GiB for blaze building blaze, 61 to 71 GB on reth and tempo); the same change fixes edits after a restart.
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: to start once the new compiler exists

decisions.decision: The optimizer's tier bars may be measured against rustc -O0, -O1 and -O3 in the optimizer's benchmark harness only. rustc stays out of every correctness path and every build.
decisions.why: A Pareto claim needs a reference point; rule verify-on-real-projects forbids rustc as an oracle, not as a stopwatch for a published benchmark.
decisions.recommended: Yes, as a narrow exception written into the rule when the harness is built.
decisions.state: decided; the rule text changes with the harness (ledger B20)

decisions.decision: Release builds keep the linker's patch room (as file holes).
decisions.why: The file-level splice that makes release edit-links fast uses it at every optimization level.
decisions.recommended: Keep.
decisions.state: in force

decisions.decision: blaze's checkout of a git dependency carries a deterministic, synthesized .git that real git can read.
decisions.why: cargo's checkout has one and build scripts (vergen) run git there; a stub that answers one command and breaks another is worse than none.
decisions.recommended: Build it as its own spec-then-build piece.
decisions.state: to start

decisions.decision: bstd's unsynced renames issue a truly unsynced rename on real drivers too.
decisions.why: That is their documented contract; callers relying on the stronger behaviour are the bugs the simulation exists to find; nothing runs on bstd yet.
decisions.recommended: Keep.
decisions.state: in force on bstd-test-1111

decisions.decision: `strip` in a profile is accepted with a named note on every build until the linker honours it (ledger D44); it is not refused.
decisions.why: Real projects set it; refusing would stop builds the reference compiler accepts.
decisions.recommended: Note, not refusal.
decisions.state: written on inv-fix-1111 and verified; to merge

decisions.decision: A missed loader probe is not part of a pure build script's key: a library appearing later at a probed path does not invalidate the kept run.
decisions.why: Same class as system libraries, which are not keyed either; tightening it needs a design for runtime inputs as a whole.
decisions.recommended: Leave and track.
decisions.state: tracked

decisions.decision: The Python fixture generator is ported once into blaze-script as its one home, together with the harness scripts that use it; loop_syscalls.py stays on the allowed list until then.
decisions.why: A second copy of the fixture in Rust would be two homes for one concept.
decisions.recommended: Port it with its users.
decisions.state: to do with the harness batch

decisions.decision: bv_decide (Lean.ofReduceBool) is allowed for bit-vector rule proofs only, in files the MIR proofs cannot import, listed by the gate.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: yes to "yes, but kept separate".
decisions.recommended: Yes, kept separate.
decisions.state: done on rule-lang-1111: the gate enforces it; 3 of 248 theorems use it

decisions.decision: Builds by the released blaze that fault (the forged-id panic, a loop stall) are retried by the VM scripts, each retry printed with its cause, until the use-after-release behind the panic is found.
decisions.why: The panic happens from a clean database, so clearing state is not a fix; a loud retry keeps work moving without hiding it.
decisions.recommended: Retry loudly; find the cause on the new compiler.
decisions.state: in force

decisions.decision: One large ix VM per concurrent heavy job (bootstrap, target projects, verification, a building lane); a VM is removed when its job ends.
decisions.why: Verification capacity, not writing, was the day's bottleneck; a 62 GB VM was OOM-killed and one VM lost its disk.
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: in force: rework-b (bootstrap), rework-t (reth, tempo), rework-d, rework-e, rework-s

decisions.decision: A branch is admin-merged to main when its own content is verified on a VM, in small pieces as each goes green, rather than held for one large merge.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: "can we admin merge anything in as well". Long-lived unmerged branches were the source of the semantic conflicts that broke main.
decisions.recommended: Merge what is verified now: the invariant controls with the strip note and the nostd port; the lint baselines; the three compiler fixes (memory budget, loader reads, effect-check binder) once stage 2 passes with them.
decisions.state: in progress

decisions.decision: The scheduler is redesigned as one graph of pure, identity-keyed nodes pulled by what is waited for: cycles as single nodes, no shared mutable state in a node, priority from who waits, cores and memory both admitted, built for hundreds of cores (docs/v2/plan/design/scheduler.md). Built in the order of measured cost, summaries and the two codegen locks first.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: "redesign the whole scheduler", "needs to work on 100s of cores". A release build of blaze by blaze kept 17 to 43 of 64 cores busy; about 30% of its CPU was one pass redone by many threads; two locks cost 6,555 thread-seconds.
decisions.recommended: Yes; keep the pool, fibers and slots of the 2026-11-02 plan and replace the model above them.
decisions.state: design merged; step 1 started

decisions.decision: build, run and test default to the edit goal: tier 0 code first, optimized code made in the background and patched in; the max goal waits for optimized code. The goal and the promotion's progress are on every status line.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: "by default we should start with a debug build and then in the background try to get more optimized, like a JIT"; Relax (makepad) publishes 50 to 200 ms save-to-patch with this shape.
decisions.recommended: Yes, as step 7 of the scheduler design; one goal setting replaces the two tier settings the tree has.
decisions.state: designed, not built

decisions.decision: A statement of fact rests on a tool call of the session; rule claims-from-evidence.
decisions.why: The agent said LLVM was most of an 80-minute build without a query; the profile said about 13%.
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: done: rule 61 on main (#2052)

decisions.decision: Interim: cargo with the pinned nightly builds, checks and unit-tests blaze in the dev loop, and a cargo-built blaze is a legal stage 0; blaze still builds blaze daily and for releases, and every claim about blaze's behaviour is measured with a blaze.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: "ideally we can build with cargo until blaze is fast". cargo check passes after three small fixes; a release build takes 292 s on the Mac against about 80 minutes and 175 GB for blaze building blaze.
decisions.recommended: Yes, with the conditions in rule blaze-builds-blaze; back to blaze-only when a warm self-rebuild is under a minute.
decisions.state: done: rule changed; the cargo-built blaze of all-1111 runs hello-world on macOS

decisions.decision: The bar is makepad's Relax, measured head to head on one machine and kept in the gate, and blaze has to be categorically better: a body edit patched in under 20 ms, a save rerunning only the tests it reaches, a cold start that is a download from a store shared across machines, optimized code faster than rustc --release, hundreds of cores, the whole language.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: "we strictly need better compile times and faster code than our competitor", "we need to be categorically better". Relax publishes 50 to 200 ms save-to-patch and optimized code 1.14 to 2.29 times slower than rustc --release.
decisions.recommended: Yes; these are targets, none is measured yet.
decisions.state: harness to build

decisions.decision: Agents first: the hub's primary interface is an API on a lane (read, write, patch, one transaction per multi-file change), with no local checkout needed. Every tree is a BLAKE3 Merkle tree and a lane is a root; sync is root comparison. A local directory with a watcher is a compatibility path; a mounted filesystem for people is out of scope.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: "what if we do it the Unison way: every single tree is a Merkle BLAKE tree", "we only really care about agents; design agent first".
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: being specified and started by the hub lane (docs/v2/plan/design/hub.md, branch hub-1111)

decisions.decision: Git stays the origin and the hub is a derived index: every object is indexed by its BLAKE3 hash and its git object id, a commit imports to a root and a lane exports as a commit, the hub speaks git's protocol for reads, and it is self-hostable. Adoption is four steps, each useful alone: blaze as a drop-in for cargo, a shared store, the hub for agent lanes, the hub's check as a required status.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: large companies have all their infrastructure on git; "we want OpenAI and other large companies to use this, what is the best way"; "ok sounds good do this".
decisions.recommended: Yes: never ask a company to leave git; losing the hub loses warmth, never work.
decisions.state: in the hub lane's brief

decisions.decision: After a design review: tier 0 code depends only on a function's own MIR and the signatures and layouts it names; optimized code is stored with a recorded trace; invalidation is pushed from the edit and the edit's chain runs on one thread; functions are reached through entry slots with code appended, never written over; the call graph's cycles are computed as an explicit query; identities become per stage. Type and borrow checking stay eager.
decisions.why: A no-code review of the plan by a second Fable at high effort, asked for by Andrew, 2026-11-11; its main finding was that the lanes then running did not follow the plan's own order (nobody was on the edit path).
decisions.recommended: Adopt all of it; the code-speed target is stated as faster than default rustc --release until measured.
decisions.state: edit-path, launcher and hub lanes started; promotion deferred

decisions.decision: While cargo builds blaze in the dev loop, a new crate that has to be verified now sits on core and alloc, not bstd, and says in its header that it moves to bstd when the rule returns to blaze-only.
decisions.why: bstd uses blaze-only syntax and features (core::reflect, blaze_comptime, for const), so rustc rejects it and a crate on it cannot be checked or tested with cargo; blaze-hub and blaze-launch were written on bstd and could not be verified. Andrew, 2026-11-11: "your decision is fine".
decisions.recommended: Yes, as an interim; the alternative was to block new crates on making bstd build under rustc.
decisions.state: in force; blaze-launch is being ported, blaze-hub is next

decisions.decision: State of the art first: design the end state and build it directly, its independent pieces in parallel lanes, then prove it on tempo and reth and in the head-to-head; rule sota-first, and rule agents-are-a-cost no longer caps lanes at four.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: "don't do things incrementally, go for SOTA right away and do things in parallel, and then try to get tempo to work".
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: done: rules changed; a lane on tempo and reth started

decisions.decision: Tests of stateful, incremental, concurrent or durable behaviour run in the deterministic simulation by default (rule simulate-first); revision tests (a project and a sequence of source revisions with state kept) are the form for incremental behaviour; a real daemon is the second, thin driver.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: "if everything is sans-IO you could just use DST", "properly bias towards sans-IO and DST"; a contributor pointed at rustc's tests/incremental revisions as the pattern.
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: rule on main; the harness is being built on revisions-1111

decisions.decision: cargo may be timed on the same program as a stopwatch reference in published comparisons (the film, the head-to-head), named plainly as cargo; it is never an oracle for correctness and never builds a project to diff against blaze's output.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-11: the comparison in the film should be "to the existing system" and "data driven"; "more comparisons".
decisions.recommended: Yes, as a second narrow exception beside D6.
decisions.state: in force; first numbers measured on hello-world

decisions.decision: The daemon stays, as a bounded cache over content-keyed store records read through the store's pool (crates/blaze-cas/src/pool): warm in memory are the workspace's memos and the pool pages read since the sweep last came by, a sealed dependency is its interface records and the code the program reaches, and the idle footprint is held to a budget that grows with the workspace, not with its dependencies. The allocator's kept memory is fixed apart from that. Not a process a run, as Relax is.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-12, as the main agent relayed it to lane memstrat-1111: "ok do everything SOTA", agreeing the daemon stays. The head-to-head (docs/v2/plan/design/restore.md, "Memory: a bounded cache over records"): Relax runs an edit in 87 to 212 MB with no process between runs, but its no-op is 52 ms where the daemon's is 12, it is incremental a crate, and its memory grows with the project.
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: steps a and c built on memstrat-1111; b and d not built

decisions.decision: The blaze edition's opt-in is the manifest's `edition = "blaze-2026.11"`, one spelling, carried to the front end as the crate attribute `#![blaze::edition = "2026.11"]`; `main` takes the roots the runtime makes in its order (`&Cx`, then `Io`), by rule `entry-takes-roots`; the entry is library code (`bstd::entry::run`) called from a module appended to the root. docs/v2/plan/design/std.md, "The blaze edition: opting in".
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-12: bstd should be what programs use, entry `fn main(io: Io)` "or whatever it is", opt-in so old things compile. A cargo-readable key lost: a package of the edition is not a cargo package. Lane bstd-entry-1112.
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: in force; slice 1 on bstd-entry-1112

decisions.decision: `blaze new` defaults to the blaze edition, and `blaze::not_latest_edition` warns by default, from the day bstd ships with blaze (std.md row S5d): one switch each, `blaze_new::BSTD_SHIPS` and `ready::EDITION_SHIPS`, both false today. Until then `blaze new --bstd <PATH>` writes the edition package, `--rust` the plain one, and the lint is `allow` unless asked for. blaze's own workspace allows the lint while cargo builds blaze (D25).
decisions.why: Andrew asked for the edition as `blaze new`'s default and a warning for packages not on it. Today a package of the edition names bstd by path into a checkout of blaze, so the default would break `blaze new` + `blaze run` on every installed blaze (the release's install check), and the warning would tell people to move to something they cannot build. Lane bstd-entry-1112; for Andrew to overrule.
decisions.recommended: Yes, until S5d; then flip both.
decisions.state: in force; for Andrew to confirm

decisions.decision: A function's error type is the exact set of failures it may return, checked like effects: the set is an error union (`A | B`, edition change 2, ledger E3), `?` widens a member or a smaller set with no `From` written, a failure the set lacks is an error naming the call, the member and the set, and a `match` covers every member. bstd's errors move onto sets: a kind variant that only holds another error (`FsKind::Stopped`, `HttpKind::Net`, `Refused::Stopped`, ...) becomes a member of the function's set (docs/v2/plan/design/error-sets.md has the list).
decisions.why: Asked for by Andrew, 2026-11-12: bstd's ~30 error types should compose, so that `fn main(cx: &Cx) -> Result<(), E>` works when one function mixes `need_fs()?` (Missing) and `open_dir()?` (FsError) with no glue. The union type and its widening were already on main (E3 parts 1 and 2); what was missing was a set as a generic argument (a parser bug), matching by member, the error's words and the proof.
decisions.recommended: Yes: a set costs what the hand-written enum costs (measured for layout), and each area keeps its own error; the alternative, one named enum per mix of areas with `From` impls, is the pattern the edition removes.
decisions.state: built and tested under cargo on branch bstd-error-sets (parser, matching by member, diagnostics, determinism and layout tests); the bstd port waits for D29; the typed binding `e: T`, the unneeded-member advice and inferred sets are not built

decisions.decision: `blaze::implicit_overflow` (edition group, allow by default) refuses integer `+ - * << >>`, unary `-`, compound forms, value-losing casts and profile-dependent or panicking calls (`pow`, `abs`, `next_power_of_two`, `sum`, `product`, `strict_*`) unless the code writes `checked_*`/`wrapping_*`/`saturating_*`/`overflowing_*`/`try_from` or the reach prover shows the operation fits. The proof treats an operation it can't show fits as fitting from then on, so the verdict is the same with and without overflow checks. `/` and `%` are excluded because their panics are the same in every profile. `blaze-std` and `blaze-mem` deny it once `bstd-fallible-alloc` (D29) lands (docs/v2/plan/design/explicit-overflow.md).
decisions.why: Asked for by Andrew, 2026-11-12: code written by LLMs should say whether arithmetic wraps, checks or saturates, denying plain `+ -` or at least linting for it.

decisions.decision: What build, run, check and test show is blaze's own, not cargo's lines: on a terminal a region redrawn while the build runs and at most one line when it ends (nothing for a run that built nothing); off a terminal `blaze: progress` every 10 s and one `blaze: ok` or `blaze: failed` line of key=value fields. `Compiling`, `Finished`, `Running`, `link:` and the per-unit `generated N warnings` and `could not compile` lines are gone; the JSON messages on stdout are unchanged. A frontier (a row a unit under way with how many wait on it) over a dependency tree or a lane a worker, from frames of recorded builds. docs/terminal.md.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-12: "can you improve the terminal output too? like `blaze run` could be more like nom + buck2 ... proper TUI thing ... reinvent, super modern"; rule useful-not-parity.
decisions.recommended: Yes. The cost: a tool that reads cargo's human lines from blaze's stderr reads nothing it knows (the harnesses filter `blaze:` lines already and read build-finished), and the `blaze check --fix` hint that the per-unit warning line carried is not said anywhere now.
decisions.state: built on termui-1112, not merged

decisions.decision: A proc-macro call whose session moved on (a stateful crate: jsonrpsee's `proc_macro_crate::CACHE`), or whose crate the store has not seen yet, has known reads when it gives, run once more from the fresh state, exactly what it gave in its session: its unit's record and its crate's image are then kept. A call that gives otherwise from the fresh state (a counter) stays unknown and its unit is made again every build, loudly (`misses` step `unit record`).
decisions.why: lane reth-1112 (claude-fable-5-2), on the owner's `make sure reth fast as fuck`: 7 units of reth were made again in every build and 217 in the first build after a cold one for this alone. What is given up: a macro that is truly order-dependent and happens to give the fresh state's output in one build has that output kept; before, nothing of such a crate was ever kept.
decisions.recommended: Yes; run blaze-macro-eval's tests/kept.rs and corpus.rs (BLAZE_MACRO_CORPUS) before it lands.
decisions.state: built on reth-1112 (77c4d94579), merged into int-1112; fixtures measured, reth being measured; the owner has not seen it

decisions.decision: A build script's run that read what can't be traced (the clock, randomness, the network) and whose script said what reruns it (`rerun-if-changed`, `rerun-if-env-changed`) is kept by cargo's rule and by what it read of its own package; what it read elsewhere (the checkout's other files through `git`, the toolchain's) is no input of it. A traceable run keeps every read, as before, and so does an untraceable one that named nothing.
decisions.why: lane reth-1112: rule useful-not-parity matches cargo where real code depends on it, and reth does: its `reth-node-core` script stamps the build time and asks `git` whether the checkout is dirty, and says in its source that debug builds must not run it again. Traced, it read 2,916 files of the checkout: every build hashed them (13 s of each edit) and every edit ran it again and remade the crates above it. What is given up: such a script is not run again when a file it read outside its package changes (the `-dirty` suffix of a version string goes stale, as under cargo).
decisions.recommended: Yes.
decisions.state: built on reth-1112 (4787b9a562), not yet measured on reth; the owner has not seen it

decisions.decision: A run with nothing changed is answered with no daemon: the thin client checks the request's slot (`<state>/slots/<key>`, blaze-certify) by lstat and execs the program; the daemon exits 600 s after the last edit (30 s if it did no work), never while a launcher is connected, and is held to D29's bound while it stays. Reverses D29's 'not a process a run'.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-12 17:52: "it needs to be better, not just 3x, but better": Relax holds nothing between runs, so a daemon that stays loses the held row whatever it holds.
decisions.recommended: Yes. The cost: the first edit after an idle exit pays a daemon start and a restore from disk.
decisions.state: written on int-1112, not compiled

decisions.decision: blaze gets its own typed SQL (docs/v2/plan/design/sql.md, rows Q1 to Q7): one sans-IO checker over a SQL subset with a schema made of Rust structs, drivers for C SQLite (libsqlite3-sys's amalgamation, no rusqlite) and Postgres (an own sans-IO wire protocol), SQL only as a const generic string, parameters named (`$name`) and bound by a record, row types computed with `type_of!`. Not wrapped: sqlx. Not forked: Turso. The work is on branch sql-1113 in its own worktree, because int-1112 does not compile and another session owns it.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-13: "make ur own sqlite thing", "be nice if it work for postgres too", "it should DENY any injection stuff i.e., should require prepared statement like things and imo should be NAMED", and "ok sounds good" to the plan; executors are Opus 5.5 medium ("doit with subagnt opus 5.5 medium not fable").
decisions.recommended: Yes. What it costs: it does nothing for the edit loop on reth and tempo; its use to blaze is as the first consumer of `type_of!`, records and field types.
decisions.state: merged to main as d46689c21e (#2119), by admin merge before its jobs ended: the checker, the SQLite driver and the Postgres core pass their tests under cargo (76, 24, 28); not yet run: blaze check and its lints, the workspace check, a long run of the refinement, a real Postgres; Q4 to Q9 (the typed surface and its language pieces) not started

decisions.decision: The fresh core (docs/v2/plan/design/target.md, interface crate crates/blaze-keyed): one process per command answers from records keyed from text before the work, each carrying the read list its work made; on a key miss the read list is checked against the current surfaces and a verified result is filed under the new key byte for byte. No daemon, no query graph, no memory admission; the memo (`RecordsOnly` for one-shot commands, `Resident` for watch and live runs) and the executor (`Local`, or a remote service) are static type parameters of one driver. Records are the unit of sharing: deterministic bytes, namespaced keys (public only for registry archives by checksum and the toolchain), segments as the wire format, signed statements. It supersedes end-state.md and end-state/*.md.
decisions.why: Decided by the main agent on the owner's instruction, 2026-11-13. The owner's priority order: "incremental comp being short > memory usage > cold comp > disk gc being good/not locking > disk usage"; "dont measure just build". Builds on the outside audit accepted 2026-11-13 (/Volumes/Projects/blaze-int-1112-notes/audit-1113.md) and target-decisions-1113.md beside it; both traces from the start because incremental time comes first and disk last.
decisions.recommended: Yes. Wave 2 (front end over surface images, body records, blaze-memo, blaze-program, blaze-expansion, test records) builds on blaze-keyed's vocabulary.

decisions.decision: Scope of the target design, as the owner answered it. In: cargo workspaces, accepted on reth, tempo and blaze; hosts macOS arm64 and Linux (arm64 first; x86-64 is CI's, no x86 VM for now); a build runs when asked and may leave a helper process with an expiry that holds only what records rebuild and never builds on its own; `run` and `build` check only what the program reaches, `check` checks everything asked; dependencies and everything from the bucket maximally optimized, workspace code fast first and tiered up in the background, the top tier optimizing across functions at function grain (keyed by its body and the keys of every body it took in); the shared cache read without a login, written only by CI and later the remote workers; fully local private builds always possible; an old home detected, reported and rebuilt, never migrated; new crates move to bstd once blaze builds blaze; long-term code sans-IO; every design aims within 10% of the floor from the start. Not now: `blaze watch` or building on save (edits come in transactions), live patching that keeps a running program's state, Windows, Buck or Bazel. Content-addressed code as in Unison, except that a body's key holds the interfaces of what it calls, not their bodies. AGENTS.md's Scope section, docs/v2/plan/design/target.md's Scope section, and rules 2, 6, 14, 20, 26, 28, 34, 60, 67 and 70 carry it. Verify once, by construction (the owner's decision 18, 16:13) is the new rule 74, verify-once, and a section of target.md. The day's general principles are rules for all code: 75 nothing-ambient, 76 correct-by-construction, 77 work-once, 78 strategy-is-a-type-parameter, 79 interfaces-first, 80 act-on-snapshots; 18 (bounded by construction) and 25 (nothing of the machine in what is kept or shared) are widened.
decisions.why: Decided by the owner, 2026-11-13 15:59 (/Volumes/Projects/blaze-int-1112-notes/target-decisions-1113.md, "Scope, as the owner answered it"), with his words that day: "10% of floor should AIM for the right thing from the start! it is ok if we don't get there but think properly; just work for something you are highly proud of even on first try likely and then iterate" and "always make sure what you build is something you are proud of ... on first iteration even".
decisions.recommended: Yes, as the owner's decision; recorded by claude-opus-5-5.

decisions.decision: blaze owns its test engine and its simulated machine (docs/v2/plan/design/sim.md, interface crate crates/blaze-sim, row V12). A test case is a function of one tape of labelled, bounded choices in which 0 is the calm choice; blaze-sim draws the tape from a seed, shrinks a failing tape, prints it and replays it from one line, and holds what the simulations copied (answers in flight, planted-bug controls, reach points). blaze stops depending on Hegel: vendor/hegeltest goes once every `#[hegel::test]`, the fresh core's hand-rolled simulations, `blaze_core::sim::Sim` and the code `#[blaze::contract_test]` generates draw from the tape. This reverses the testing skill's "moving to Hegel's own `hegel::sim`". Nothing is taken as a dependency from indexable-inc/hegel; its design (every choice a draw, 0 calm, a disk in three layers) is prior art.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-13: on the plan to move the simulation into `hegel::sim`, "reverse yea and just make dst as good as possible"; then, told that `hegel::sim` is on the fork's main and was never pinned here, "i think dont use indexable-inc/hegel dont depend on hegel nayrmoe jsut contro ldirectly in blaze (use opus 5.5)". Found that day on main at e6635c9ba7: every simulation's schedule is one opaque seed that Hegel cannot shrink; `Sim`, blaze-check and the fresh core's loops are three machines that do not meet; 14 draw traits, 92 `enum Plant` and 21 control helpers are copies; the vendored engine is about 128,000 lines pinned 13 commits behind its fork, and bstd cannot depend on it.
decisions.recommended: Yes. What it costs: a port of 354 tests in 70 crates and of the compiler's contract-test code generation, and a shrinker blaze now maintains. What is given up from Hegel: generation from a regular expression (10 uses) and its targeted search (not used here).
